title: Bhishma waits for the sun
hookLine: a warrior on a bed of arrows waits for the sun to turn north; why families save good beginnings for after Sankranti
carry: uttarayana: the sun's bright half, when good things begin
last: RAKSHA BANDHAN: A PROMISE YOU KEEP.

cards: The great war of the Mahabharata, and the oldest warrior on the field goes down. Bhishma, great-uncle to both sides, is struck by so many arrows that when he falls, he never touches the ground. He lies on them like a bed.
And Bhishma has a gift, a boon from long ago: he can choose the moment he dies. The pain is enormous. The war goes on around him.
Everyone expects him to let go. He doesn't. He looks up at the sky and says he'll wait.

teach.b: For weeks Bhishma lies there, and he doesn't waste the time. The family comes to him, and he teaches them about duty, kingship and God. Then the sun turns north, and only then does he let go.
Because the sun's northward half of the year, uttarayana, is held to be the bright, auspicious half: the best time to begin things, and a blessed time to leave the world.
The day many Hindus mark that turn is Makar Sankranti. Sankranti means crossing: the sun crossing into Makara, the sign called Capricorn. Most festivals follow the moon, so their dates wander.
This one follows the sun, so it lands in mid-January almost every year. Here's the teaching. For Hindus, time isn't all the same.
Some times are shubh, auspicious, good for beginning, and families look up a muhurat, an auspicious moment, for a wedding, a new house, a first day.

In many North Indian families, weddings pause in the month before Sankranti and start again once the sun has turned. And in Gujarat, whole cities climb onto their rooftops that day and fill the sky with kites.
The old texts don't mention kites; the rooftops do. Some say they're thanks sent up toward the sun. And today: when your family waits for a good date, it isn't just superstition.
It's the idea Bhishma held on for.
What you begin, begin in the light.

how: On Makar Sankranti, in mid-January, many Hindus bathe in rivers, give to those in need, share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Gujarat and elsewhere spend the day flying kites from rooftops to mark the sun's turn north into uttarayana, the auspicious half of the year when many families plan weddings and new beginnings.

games.q: you're Bhishma. you've fallen, you lie on a bed of arrows, and you can choose the moment of your death. what do you do?
o: go now and end the pain.
wait for the sun to turn north.
games.why: he waits for weeks, teaching, until uttarayana, the bright half, begins. only then does he let go.

practice: Sit where there's daylight if you can, or picture winter sun on your face. Think of one thing you'd like to begin: a habit, a conversation, a piece of work. Don't start it yet.

Just hold it, the way Bhishma held on, and choose a moment to begin it, a morning, a day, on purpose. If you pray, offer it to the sun with folded hands, the way many Hindus greet Surya at dawn. Then breathe out slowly.
